recalcitrant

rih-KAL-sih-trunt · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Recalcitrant is stubbornly resistant to authority or control.

The committee struggled for months to negotiate with the recalcitrant union representative, who rejected every proposed compromise.

Worked Example

Despite years of therapy, the recalcitrant patient still refused to follow even the simplest parts of his treatment plan.

Recalcitrant describes someone (or something) that digs in and resists control, often stubbornly and repeatedly.

Your Turn

Answer correctly to continue.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

defiant: Defiant means openly resisting authority, and it points at a moment -- a defiant refusal is loud, direct, and dramatic. Recalcitrant is about stubbornness over time: a recalcitrant person keeps resisting through every attempt to correct or persuade them, with or without any open scene.

unruly: Unruly means hard to control or discipline, and unruly disorder is often aimless -- an unruly crowd may simply be chaotic. Recalcitrant resistance is deliberate and directed: a recalcitrant person understands exactly what authority wants and stubbornly keeps refusing to give it.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

obedient: willing to follow rules or instructions

yielding: willing to give in or comply

Where it sits · how actively authority is defied — reluctant → recalcitrant → rebellious

reluctant vs. recalcitrant: Reluctant is far milder than recalcitrant: a reluctant person is merely unwilling and slow to act, but usually gives in, while a recalcitrant one keeps refusing no matter how often he is pressed.

rebellious vs. recalcitrant: Rebellious goes a step beyond recalcitrant: a recalcitrant person digs in and resists control, while a rebellious one openly fights the authority itself, often as part of a larger uprising.

Build the Word

The pieces

prefix — re-

prefix — re-: back (Latin)

root — calcitr-

root — calcitr-: to kick (from Latin calcitrare, built on calx, 'heel')

suffix — -ant

suffix — -ant: inclined to; forms an adjective (Latin)

Put it together

Put it together: Recalcitrant is built from re- ('back') + calcitr- ('to kick,' from Latin calcitrare, itself built on calx, 'heel') + -ant (an adjective ending) -- it literally means 'kicking back.' That heel root survives today only in the rare anatomical word calcaneus (heel bone), too uncommon for a fair quiz here -- but it's a fun fact worth keeping.

Use the root in a new word: calcaneus

Use the root in a new word: calcaneus: The X-ray showed a hairline fracture in the runner's calcaneus, the large bone that forms the heel.

Strength Check

Word Choice

Recalcitrant is most often used for someone who keeps resisting despite repeated attempts to correct or persuade them -- it implies stubbornness over time, not just a single refusal.
